subChunks.title: Joining Two Tables — INNER JOIN
subChunks.hookHtml: Foreign keys link tables in theory. INNER JOIN brings that linked data back together in a single query result.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Syntax

SELECT a.name, a.xp, m.name AS mentor
FROM   apprentices AS a
INNER JOIN mentors AS m ON a.mentor_id = m.id;

The ON clause specifies the join condition — usually foreign_key = primary_key. The INNER JOIN returns only rows where the condition matches in both tables.

What rows are excluded

Apprentices with mentor_id = NULL (no mentor) are excluded — NULL never matches. Mentors with no apprentices are also excluded.

Table aliases are essential

-- Ambiguous — which table's 'name'?
SELECT name FROM apprentices INNER JOIN mentors ON ...

-- Unambiguous:
SELECT a.name, m.name AS mentor_name
FROM apprentices AS a
INNER JOIN mentors AS m ON a.mentor_id = m.id;

Joining on non-id columns

You can join on any columns with compatible values, not just id columns. But joining on primary key ↔ foreign key is by far the most common pattern.

storyBeats.text: 'Give me each apprentice's name alongside their mentor's name,' says the Headmaster. Two ledgers, one answer.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: INNER JOIN brings matching rows from two tables together into one result. Rows that do not match on both sides disappear. Apprentices with no mentor vanish. Mentors with no apprentices vanish. Only matched pairs survive.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what INNER JOIN does, which rows are excluded, and why table aliases are important when joining.

options: Only rows where the join condition matches in both tables
All rows from the left table, with NULLs for unmatched right rows
All rows from both tables regardless of matching
The Cartesian product of both tables
questions.answer: Only rows where the join condition matches in both tables
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN is the intersection of the two tables on the join condition. Rows that do not match on both sides are excluded from the result.

questions.prompt: Using the lesson data, how many rows does the INNER JOIN of apprentices and mentors return?
options: 4 (Alice, Bjorn, Cassia, Elara — Dorian and Fenrir have NULL mentor_id)
questions.answer: 4 (Alice, Bjorn, Cassia, Elara — Dorian and Fenrir have NULL mentor_id)
questions.explanation: Dorian and Fenrir have mentor_id = NULL. NULL never matches any value, so those rows are excluded from the INNER JOIN result. Four apprentices have non-NULL mentor_ids that match existing mentors.

options: The condition that links rows from the two tables — match apprentice.mentor_id with mentor.id
The primary key of the joined result
A filter applied after the join like WHERE
The column order of the result
questions.answer: The condition that links rows from the two tables — match apprentice.mentor_id with mentor.id
questions.explanation: The ON clause is the join predicate. It tells the engine which rows from each table correspond to each other. The most common form is foreign_key = primary_key.

questions.prompt: Both tables have a column called `name`. A developer writes `SELECT name FROM apprentices INNER JOIN mentors ON ...`. What happens?
options: An error or ambiguous column error — the engine does not know which table's name column to use
The apprentice name is returned by default
The mentor name is returned by default
Both name columns are returned automatically
questions.answer: An error or ambiguous column error — the engine does not know which table's name column to use
questions.explanation: When two joined tables share a column name, you must qualify it with the table alias: SELECT a.name, m.name. Without qualification the engine raises an ambiguous column reference error.
